catalog_quote: Main stress is regularly on the first vowel of a word. Where the first vowel has zero realisation as in, for example, the optional pronunciation [gwá.ɾo] of /guwadu/ 'crab' (M), the stress is on the second vowel (which is, of course, the first vocoid). Length in a non-initial vowel (because it is phonemically long or because it is followed by a glide and its homorganic vowel, which sequence may be realised as a diphthong) results in an apparent stress which may sometimes detract from the regular stress on the first vowel, thus [bɪyá:lku] /biya:lku/ 'hunt (purposive)'. new_statements.rule_in_words: Primary stress falls on the first vowel (first syllable) of every word, in both dialects (Margany and Gunya). If the first vowel is phonetically elided (e.g. /guwadu/ pronounced [gwá.ro]) the stress sits on the first vowel actually realised. A phonemically long or diphthongal non-initial vowel (especially /a:/) can carry an 'apparent' stress that competes with the initial one.
new_statements.secondary_stress: p. 296: 'There may be a secondary stress on the third syllable of a four syllable word especially if the word is a reduplication or a compound form. The third syllable will not be stressed if the second is stressed by virtue of its length' (examples G. [gábalgàbal] 'old man', [dátubìra] 'waddy', [bádinìya] 'I am sick'). 'When a word is of five or more syllables a secondary stress will appear on the first syllable of a non-initial disyllabic or longer morpheme or, where the bound morphemes are all monosyllabic, on the first or second of these (the rule for predicting which is not known).' Unclear whether an initial long-vowel syllable counts as two syllables for stress; 'probably does' ([gú:mùndu] 'from the nose').
new_statements.exceptions: Apparent stress on long non-initial vowels (esp. /a:/, as in /biya:lku/); 'rare examples in sentences of irregular stress on non-initial vowels' with insufficient evidence (e.g. [gámumugálgiya] 'I'm going to get water', G); the verb waba (M)/wadya (G) 'go' is often phonologically incorporated with preceding ugu 'hither' and not stressed as a separate word ([úguwaba] 'come here'). Phonetic bracket forms in the quote are approximations of the typewritten IPA in the scan (checked against the page image).
new_statements.domain_note: Word-level stress in isolated words/elicited forms; the section is written jointly for the two dialects Margany (M) and Gunya (G) with examples labelled by dialect. Intonation is treated separately in §2.5 (p. 296-297): statement = final fall; a strongly stressed word in a statement may carry high tone. Breen notes the corpus contains almost no fluent text.
new_statements.identity_note: Breen 1981 treats Margany (marg1253) and Gunya (guny1241) as two dialects of one unnamed Mari (Maric) language and writes the phonology, including §2.4 Stress, jointly for both, marking examples (M) or (G); the stress rule is stated once for the language and illustrated with Gunya forms ([gábalgàbal] 'old man', [bádinìya] 'I am sick', [wádyeyindàna] 'they are going'). Gunya data come from speakers of the southern part of Gunya territory (Cunnamulla area; the McKellar family). StressTyp2 files the same statement under 'Margany' only. Wikipedia and AIATSIS treat Gunya as a dialect of the Bidjara cluster (bidy1243).

sources.note: Section 2.4 Stress, pp. 295-296 (PDF pp. 316-317): main stress regularly on the first vowel of the word; optional secondary stress on the 3rd syllable of 4-syllable words and on morpheme-initial syllables in 5+ syllable words; long non-initial vowels give an 'apparent stress'; rare irregular non-initial stress in sentences. Statement covers both dialects, examples marked (M) Margany and (G) Gunya.
